questions.q: Explain what an overflow error is.

markPoints.concept: the result of a calculation needs more bits than are available
accept: more bits|too many bits|more than|too big|too large|exceeds|does not fit|will not fit|9 bits|nine bits
markPoints.exemplar: The answer needs more bits than the computer has set aside.

markPoints.concept: so the extra bit is lost and the stored answer is wrong
accept: wrong|incorrect|inaccurate|not the right answer|wrong answer|wrong result|wrong value|wrong number
markPoints.exemplar: The extra bit is lost, so the stored answer is wrong.

questions.example: An overflow happens when the result of a calculation needs more bits than are available — for example a ninth bit in an 8-bit system. The extra bit cannot be stored, so it is lost and the answer the computer keeps is wrong.
questions.paraphrase: It occurs when an answer is too big for the number of bits allowed, and because the top bit has nowhere to go the result that gets stored is incorrect.
questions.feedback: Too big for the space, then what that costs.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 8 — Binary workshop, station 5: Overflow

questions.q: Add these two 8-bit binary numbers: 11101101 + 01011011. Give the 8 bits that would be stored.
questions.feedback: 237 + 91 = 328, which needs nine bits. Only the lower eight are stored, giving 01001000 — 72, not 328. That is an overflow error.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 8 — Binary workshop, station 5: Overflow

questions.q: An 8-bit system adds 10110101 and 11001100. What happens?
options: An overflow error: the answer needs nine bits
The answer is stored correctly as an 8-bit number
The computer automatically switches to 16 bits
The two numbers are swapped and added again
questions.feedback: 181 + 204 = 385, which will not fit in eight bits.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 8 — Binary workshop, station 5: Overflow

questions.q: Explain why changing the most significant bit of an 8-bit number changes it by far more than changing the least significant bit.

markPoints.concept: the most significant bit is worth 128 and the least significant 1
markPoints.exemplar: The most significant bit is worth 128 and the least significant bit is worth 1.

markPoints.concept: so each place to the left is worth twice the one to its right
accept: double|doubles|twice|times two|doubling|power|powers of two|each place|every place
markPoints.exemplar: This is because each place to the left is worth twice the one to its right.

questions.example: Each place in a binary number is worth twice the place to its right, so an 8-bit number runs 128, 64, 32, 16, 8, 4, 2, 1. Flipping the left-hand bit changes the value by 128; flipping the right-hand one changes it by 1.
questions.paraphrase: Every column is double the one beside it, so the leftmost position carries 128 while the rightmost carries only 1.
questions.feedback: The two place values, and the doubling that produces them.
questions.revisitLabel: 1.2 Lesson 8 — Binary workshop, station 3: MSB and LSB
